articles.title_orig: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.title_zh: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Huang "fully supports" the investigation and is "committed to cooperating with it," the company said.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.title_zh: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship
Europe live – latest updates
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

articles.title_orig: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
articles.title_zh: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

articles.title_orig: E-Bike Rides Will Be Cheaper Next Year for Citi Bike Members in New York
articles.title_zh: E-Bike Rides Will Be Cheaper Next Year for Citi Bike Members in New York
articles.content_orig:
Lyft will cap the Citi Bike member cost of any sub-45-minute e-bike trip at $3.65 starting on Jan. 19, Mayor Mamdani said on Monday, and the bike-share provider has also agreed to freeze member rates through the middle of 2029.
The Citi Bike-loving mayor’s announcement — first reported in the New York Times —comes ahead of a City Council hearing on Citi Bike fees scheduled for Dec. 2. All four bills on the meeting’s agenda would offer discount rides or cap rider fees. Council Speaker Julie Menin is scheduled to appear at the mayor’s Citi Bike announcement on Monday morning.
Lyft made $24 million off the bike-share system last year; Transportation Alternatives’ “Citi Bike Riders Union” campaign calls on the city to cap all e-bike rides at $3. Annual membership, meanwhile, has skyrocketed from $95 in 2013 to $239 today. Citi Bike’s only existing e-bike ride price cap is $5.40 for sub-45-minute trips into or out of Manhattan; a 45-minute e-bike ride not going into or out of Manhattan currently costs $12.15.
The company’s contract to run the city’s bike-share program expires on May 26, 2029, though no competitor could likely come close to meeting the capacity demands of the current Citi Bike system. That gives Lyft significant leverage in negotiations with the city.
Editor’s note: This story initially misreported that the new price cap will apply to e-bike trips into our out of Manhattan; it will apply to all e-bike trips.

Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jim Beam’s decision to temporarily pause operations at its Kentucky distillery on America Reports.
Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories.
The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported.
However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal.

Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs.

The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future.
In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
articles.title_zh: SpaceX sued by Oregon and Virginia over AI deepfake porn, Grok safety claims
articles.content_orig:
Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator.
Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others.
In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content.
Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images.
"This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation."
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products.
SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California.
In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction.
When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content.
SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions."
The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company.
Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance.
State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms.
In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

Nvidia's board ⁠had ‌approached Haas in its search ⁠for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times reported earlier this month, following Huang's exit amid revelations of extramarital affairs ‌including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Analysts had also pointed to Haas ​as a solid candidate for the CEO role at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company, rising to ⁠vice president and general manager of its computing products ‌business, before joining Arm in ‌2013.
Haas became the British chipmaker's chief executive in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets ⁠through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year.
Arm licenses ⁠processor designs used across smartphones, ⁠PCs, servers and connected devices.

Middle powers had a middling moment
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for middle power cooperation raised expectations for 2026, but the Asia Power Index shows a mixed picture.
In a speech delivered at the World Economic Forum in January, Mark Carney declared a rupture in the rules-based order, entreating middle powers to act together to forge flexible, issue-based coalitions rather than relying on dominant superpowers. 1 He called on like-minded middle powers, such as Australia, Japan, and South Korea, to seize the initiative and shape the emerging order. However, their performance over the year proved uneven.
Australia’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 31.7 points, but its Economic Relationships score rose. This was driven by gains in Economic Diplomacy, where it climbed three places to fourth, particularly in its economic statecraft. Expert respondents praised Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s ability to advance Australia’s economic interests, reflecting his successful regional visits to secure petroleum and fertiliser supplies in the wake of the Iran war. However, they rated him less effective at advancing Australia’s diplomatic interests in Asia: more than a third of respondents gave lower appraisals than in 2025, pulling his score down 14 points to 76. The fall contributed to a modest decline in Australia’s overall Diplomatic Influence.
Japan’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 38.6 points. Yet, for the first time in the Index’s history, it improved on all four resource measures, including a first-ever rise in its Economic Capability. Its Cultural Influence also rose, largely on the back of its growth as an education destination. But these gains could not offset a further slide in Economic Relationships, where its score fell 15 per cent to a record low of 31.2. For the first time since the inception of the Index, Japan is not the primary foreign investor in any other Index country, down from three in the previous edition. An $8 billion increase in Chinese investment into Thailand and burgeoning bilateral tech investment between Taiwan and the United States meant Japan lost its status as the top investor in these three countries. As a result, Japan dropped out of the top three economic partners, and Singapore moved ahead. Experts judged Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to be a more effective leader at the global level than her predecessor, Shigeru Ishiba, but rated her regional leadership less highly. Japan’s score on that indicator fell nearly 9 points to its lowest level yet of 81.
South Korea had a difficult 2026. Its comprehensive power score fell to 31 points, with declines in five of the eight measures: Economic and Military Capability, Economic Relationships, Defence Networks, and Diplomatic Influence. Its relationship with a more transactional United States came under strain, with President Trump calling for cuts to combined military exercises. The shakier alliance has weighed on assessments of South Korea’s Military Capability, with experts less confident in its armed forces’ ability to fight a ground war. Compounding this, President Lee Jae Myung is seen as less able to manage President Trump, weakening perceptions of his regional leadership and his ability to advance South Korea’s economic interests. The country’s cultural appeal, however, is as strong as ever, with the long-term growth of K-Pop and K-Dramas complementing its growing reputation as a tourist destination.
That all three countries lost Diplomatic Influence this year calls into question their ability to shape the international system.
While the picture for like-minded middle powers is mixed, Pakistan punched above its weight in 2026, rising 0.6 points to reach a comprehensive power score just above 15 (the threshold for middle powers). Its shuttle diplomacy gave it a brief role in US–Iran ceasefire talks, culminating in the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
Experts rated Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s regional and global leadership much more highly as a result, lifting Pakistan’s Diplomatic Influence 2.8 points to 35.6. However, the Memorandum fell short of its key aim — a final deal to end the conflict — and failed to prevent the renewal of hostilities, which resumed within a month of its signing. Pakistan is unlikely to sustain this score in future editions.

articles.title_orig: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
articles.title_zh: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
articles.content_orig:
Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense . Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.
While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16 , with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.
Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.
Asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the new Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.
Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.
Asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.
This is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.
Nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.
It’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.
The machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.
The 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.
The trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively new thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That said, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.
The keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).
Unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.
Since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.
There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.
With an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).
Nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.
But these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.
The nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?

articles.title_orig: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.title_zh: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.content_orig:
Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says .
Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.
It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.
The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".
Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.
Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.
A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.
"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."
Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.
"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

articles.title_orig: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.title_zh: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.content_orig:
Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey .
Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.
They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced."
Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV , one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.
Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV company was placed under compulsory administration.
It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel , and the leading digital news website, T24.
Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, said that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.
Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a new YouTube channel.
Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news."
In the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.
According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.
This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

articles.title_orig: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
articles.title_zh: COP31: What next after UN climate talks collapse
articles.content_orig:
United Nations climate talks have ended in collapse after countries deadlocked over the phasing out of planet-warming fossil fuels, aiding energy transition for developing countries and the response to natural disasters.
Known as COP31, the conference in Antalya, Turkiye, ended on Sunday as the European Union and others ⁠⁠rejected a final deal they said was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.
The longest UN climate summit on record brought to the fore the divide between major polluters driving climate change and smaller nations bearing the brunt of its impact, after a year of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Asia .
It also laid bare the world’s inability to keep the Paris Agreement pledge to limit global warming to the 1.5C (2.7F) mark , which scientists expect to overshoot in a few years.
So what’s next for the fraught UN process and what else can nations do to deliver promises that have too often missed their target?
The 11-day-long negotiations that began on November 9 were stalled after oil-producing states blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels in the final deal put forward by the president of COP31, Turkiye, and main negotiator Australia.
Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) opposed any mention of a fossil fuel phase-out, while insisting instead on carbon capture , the technology criticised as costly and ineffective.
Cosima Cassel, programme lead in Climate Diplomacy and Geopolitics at ⁠⁠environmental think tank E3G, said petrostates attempted to slow momentum on the energy transition “following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and the projected decline in their incomes as global demand for fossil fuels falls”.
The European Union and several nations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the ⁠⁠main driver of global warming.
The revised text of a deal that emerged early on Sunday was angrily rejected after some 130 nations sent a letter to the presidency stating that a deal would have to mention a path for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
On the contrary, the text made no mention of fossil fuels while promoting carbon capture.
“A small group of blockers set the outcome against the clear position of a large majority,” Cassel told Al Jazeera. “These dynamics raise questions about the role of oil and gas exporters in undermining the only forum where vulnerable countries get to advance their concerns.”
Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on the funds needed to help them transition their energy systems and respond to natural disasters.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement , developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations. However, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine strained national budgets, leaving wealthy nations unwilling to commit trillions of dollars in climate finance.
Sebastien Duyck, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL), said wealthy developed countries, which denounced the obstruction by fossil fuel-producing nations, showed “considerable hypocrisy”.
“You cannot demand a just transition from others while failing to pay your fair share of its costs,” Duyck told Al Jazeera. “We need less finger-pointing and political theatre and more accountability. All major economies, particularly the wealthiest, must deliver on their existing legal obligations and climate finance commitments ahead of COP32.”
The collapse of the climate talks in Turkiye has renewed questions about reform of its consensus-based process, centred around the principle that all countries must agree to the reforms.
The commitment to moving away from fossil fuels – including natural gas, coal and crude oil – was considered a landmark achievement of COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. But even then, the deal stopped short of calling for a “phase-out”, amid fierce lobbying from oil-producing countries.
Amid concern that fossil fuel producers wield more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world, many believe the COP process remains important as a platform that brings together virtually every country in the world.
“The UN process remains the only forum where every country has a voice and a chance to shape outcomes and it is worth protecting and fighting for,” said E3G’s Cassel.
However, calls for reform are multiplying and a second tier of COPs – the Global Climate Action Agenda – is rising in prominence. Often called just the Action Agenda, the voluntary implementation pillar of the UN Climate Change process is bringing in real-world actors such as financial institutions, cities, regions, businesses and civil society on a voluntary basis.
“That spirit of collaboration stands in stark contrast to the adversarial dynamics that too often dominate the formal negotiations,” Cassel said.
Other routes are also being pursued. An International Court of Justice advisory opinion last year confirmed that states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change. In April, the Santa Marta initiative convened 57 countries to promote non-binding cooperation around fossil fuel phase-out.
Duyck, at CIEL, said “the failure of governments to agree at this conference does not make the science any less clear or their legal obligations any less binding.” “A fair and orderly transition away from fossil fuels remains both an imperative and a collective responsibility,” he added.
The UN Environment Programme last year said the world would exceed the 1.5C (2.7F) mark – the internationally agreed-upon target set under the Paris Agreement – “very likely” within the next decade.
Without any meaningful action, the planet will warm 2.3 to 2.5C (4.1 to 4.5F) by 2100, the report said.
Joeri Rogelj, professor of climate science and Policy at Imperial College London, said a starting point would have been to renew commitments made at COP28 in Dubai, where nations had agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, triple renewable energy capacity globally and double the global average annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030.
Instead, “even simply echoing these agreed outcomes was politically too challenging for some countries with strong vested interests in fossil fuels,” he told Al Jazeera.
“The commitments needed are clear: global greenhouse gas emissions must decline to slow the rate of global warming,” Rogelj told Al Jazeera.
“This failure risks further delaying meaningful global emissions reductions, with the poorest and most vulnerable countries and communities bearing the greatest consequences.”

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI 01.002.002 Update Has Started Rolling Out, But Some Users Will Reportedly Have to Wait 6 Hours To Get It
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI 01.002.002 Update Has Started Rolling Out, But Some Users Will Reportedly Have to Wait 6 Hours To Get It
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI has only just been released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S , but Rockstar Games isn't sitting idly on its laurels, as a new patch has started rolling out across both systems, although some users will have to wait 6 more hours until they can download it.
As reported by PlayStation Game Size , a new 1.002.002 patch started rolling out earlier today, but it seems like it will be released in three different waves. 33% of users can download it now; 66% will be able to download it in 3 hours, and all users should be able to download it in 6 hours.
This is a rather unique approach to releasing updates, but considering the success of Grand Theft Auto VI , a staggered release makes quite a lot of sense to avoid overloading the PlayStation and Xbox online services with a massive number of simultaneous downloads.
Unfortunately, we still don't know what this first Grand Theft Auto VI post-launch update does, as Rockstar Games has yet to share official patch notes. Given the 603 MB / 1.60 GB sizes on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S for the update and its quick release, major changes shouldn't be expected. As there are a few notable bugs and exploits users can take advantage of to break progression and unlock a first-person mode that seems all but ready, it's likely Rockstar Games is focusing on these issues before moving on to bigger additions.
Among the Grand Theft Auto VI glitches we have seen in these first few days of availability is an Xbox Series X|S exclusive glitch that uses Quick Resume to unlock the framerate . While gameplay is sped up, making the game unplayable, cutscenes work quite well, providing yet another indication that gameplay logic is tied to framerate.

articles.title_orig: US Stock Futures Bounce After AI-Driven Correction: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Stock Futures Bounce After AI-Driven Correction: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities surged on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, reviving the artificial intelligence trade and pushing major indexes higher after all three major market averages ended Friday in a correction.
The S&P 500 added 4%, and the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1,186 points, or 2.5%.
Nvidia soared 30% after the company's board returned Jensen Huang as the head of the company , effective immediately. President Donald Trump applauded the move, telling CNBC that "he did nothing wrong."
"He had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong other than he created a chip that's invaluable, many chips that are invaluable," he said in an interview on " Squawk on the Street ."
The stock had gotten a bit of a boost earlier in the day after Trump said in a separate post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia's board rehires Huang as CEO. Huang had resigned earlier this month after reportedly engaging in a number of extramarital affairs, one of which was with an alleged Chinese spy.
Other stocks in the AI trade jumped in sympathy with Nvidia on Monday. Micron Technology added 14%, while CoreWeave skyrocketed 29%. Advanced Micro Devices was up 9%. "Magnificent Seven" members Microsoft and Meta Platforms gained 3% each, while Alphabet popped 4%.
"Jensen Huang's return restores and rebuilds confidence in the AI ecosystem: its major suppliers, its core building blocks, and its demand outlook," said Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager and research analyst at Gabelli Funds.
To be sure, the trade "still has to push through a lot of noise about financing, geopolitics, durability and skepticism, even though companies across the AI supply chain keep reporting strong demand," Susanto added.
The moves mark a massive turnaround for the tech sector following last week's sell-off , as worries about the AI trade continued to spook investors despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.
By the end of last week — the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in a correction, down 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq was lower for the year.
The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday close to a bear market, down almost 20% from its latest high.
Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1 p.m. ET.

Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship
Europe live – latest updates
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

articles.title_zh: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive

Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

articles.title_zh: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.content_orig:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space : very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.
Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.
These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.
As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit , we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.
Sign Up for Our Newsletter
Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit , extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.
Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years , those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density . Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth , requiring more satellites for broader coverage.
Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits . Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.
Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks , reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation , should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.
The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits .
It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit , proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.
Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit , and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”
China’s clearest attempt to turn very low Earth orbit into a surveillance layer is the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation. Announced in 2023, Chutian’s bullet-shaped satellites house many types of remote sensing payloads , with onboard data processing and intersatellite links to coordinate as one network. After at least three successful demonstrations, the company aims for 300 satellites by 2030 and potentially more than 500 thereafter. The constellation is designed to observe any point on Earth as frequently as every 15 minutes — a rate which would allow the People’s Liberation Army to compress its sensor-to-shooter timeline.
The most ambitious plan comes from Hangsheng Satellite, a commercial satellite manufacturer. In August 2026, Hangsheng announced plans to build a 1,920-satellite very low Earth orbit communications and computing constellation . Its plan calls for two demonstrations in 2027, then 24 validation satellites before scaling deployment through 2030 — a demanding manufacturing and launch schedule. But once deployed, the constellation would combine stronger radiofrequency links with very low Earth orbit’s resilience to debris and persistent nuclear radiation, creating a more survivable communications and computing layer. In a conflict that disrupted low Earth orbit, such an architecture could give the Chinese military another layer through which to process, fuse, and distribute information.
Chinese startups are also pursuing very low Earth orbit. In December 2024, AIRSAT, a spin-out of the state-run Aerospace Information Research Institute, launched Haishao-1, China’s first very low Earth orbit synthetic aperture radar satellite . Operating as low as 300 kilometers, its orbit concentrates coverage on the South China Sea and Taiwan, enabling up to 5.7 times more daily observations of the region than current Chinese synthetic aperture radar satellites. Another startup, C-Space, is developing a 48-satellite imagery constellation , alongside communications and navigation capabilities .
China is also coordinating its ambitions through a very low Earth orbit industry alliance chaired by the Chinese Academy of Sci
